column3: It is the closest parallel: Job calls his Lord after harm has touched him, while adding the Satan-attribution wording.
It contrasts Job's plea with the person who calls in harm but misattributes a later gift to personal knowledge.
It states that no one but God can uncover harm and joins that authority to unrepelled favor and mercy.
Zechariah's direct call to his Lord supplies a nearby prophetic model of petition within the same sequence.
Lot's rescue and granted judgment do not materially clarify Job's harm or his plea for mercy.
It places mercy after an affliction and shows a contrary response of scheming against the signs.
It exactly shares the appeal to the Lord as the best of those who show mercy, adding forgiveness to the petition.
Noah's answered call and rescue from great distress extend the local sequence of deliverance after prayer.
The paired names of the All-Merciful and Merciful provide the broad divine quality invoked in Job's address.
It shares the exact superlative of mercy and frames mercy as a place of admission after fracture and fault.

Noah's appeal over his son is a distinct petition and adds little to Job's affliction and mercy.

The general command to seek forgiveness with divine mercy adds little after the more direct prayers.

Solomon's commanded wind and blessed land do not add to Job's affliction narrative.
The perfection of the All-Merciful's creation is too general to illuminate the petition.

Zechariah's answered petition and the posture of hopeful, fearful prayer extend the local pattern of response.
It connects prior calling with God's gracious mercy, but without a pressure or deliverance scene.
It denies that the messenger independently controls benefit or harm, reinforcing the limitation behind turning to God.
Affliction that does not produce humility or supplication provides a contrary response to Job's call.
The general statement of God's repentance, forgiveness, and mercy does not add a distinct connection.

Solomon's subjected workers are unrelated to Job's harmed condition and prayer.
God's forgiving mercy and delayed punishment are relevant divine qualities but not Job's relief from harm.
The list of prophets includes Job, yet only establishes his place among recipients of revelation.
It explicitly joins mercy and removal of harm, while showing the contrary persistence in rebellion after relief.
The messenger's lack of control over harm and guidance is only a general boundary around divine agency.
An appeal for help that receives a direct divine answer offers a distinct collective model of answered distress.
Job is included among those characterized by patience, adding a relevant local trait without treating the plea itself.
Hardship and suffering are presented as means that might bring communities to humble supplication.

The request for rescue by divine mercy makes mercy the means of deliverance from an opposing people.

Mary and her son as a sign do not clarify Job's plea.
